prize_parts.citation: For a body of work that renews lyric, essay and the verse-novel through a sustained dialogue with antiquity, joining formal invention to elegiac and erotic intensity.

statement.case_for: Carson's voice is distinctive and hard to mistake. She uses the book itself as an instrument: Autobiography of Red reworks the Geryon material as a verse novel, and Nox builds an elegy as an object. In both, formal invention is bound to grief and desire rather than being ornament. Her essays and her work on Greek texts form one continuous practice of making ancient material speak in a contemporary idiom. That gives the oeuvre intellectual depth and a clear linguistic project. She writes in English, so I am not judging her through translation, which is not true of most other shortlisted candidates. Publication over several decades shows a developing practice rather than a single breakthrough. On the common criteria (voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, depth, significance across the body of work) I find the case strongest here. It is a judgment from public knowledge, not a fresh reading of the corpus.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Carlberg, Mattson and Olsson raise in different ways. Part of the corpus consists of translations, adaptations and scholarly writing, and a citation must separate original literary work from it. The most radical books are allusive, fragmentary and sometimes dependent on physical form, so the weight of the case rests on a limited number of titles. Whether the hybrid format has lasting canonical weight, rather than influence among peers, remains open. Cărtărescu's large, sustained imaginative architecture has a scale that Carson's work does not attempt. If the committee reads the will's 'ideal direction' as favoring that kind of epic ambition, my preference could reasonably be overturned.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first for a coherent inner world built from memory, the body and cosmology through linguistic and structural invention. He ranks Carson second and notes that her translation and classical-scholarship component is hard to separate from original creation, and that her genre-crossing work needs discussion against the will's wording.
responses.response: I accept the difficulty over the translation and scholarship boundary, and I would handle it in the citation. It should credit the original poetry, verse narrative and essays, with the classical versions as context and not as part of the credited achievement. I also take seriously his argument that Cărtărescu's strength is coherence at very large scale, and I ranked him second for that reason. I still prefer Carson because her formal range is wider and I can judge her prose in the original, whereas the density and sentence-level patterning of the Romanian prose reach me only through translation. I do not regard the difference as large, and I would not object if the committee moved to Cărtărescu on the question of epic scale.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for an unmistakable voice and encyclopedic yet personal vision. She ranks Carson third, partly because the range of modes makes a single central achievement hard to define, and because it is not yet settled which of the formal experiments will endure.
responses.response: I agree that Carson's breadth makes the citation harder to write, and that the canonical weight of the hybrid books is not settled. I would argue the central achievement is the reinvention of the poetic and essayistic book as a vehicle for elegy and desire, and that this is visible across several decades rather than in one title. I concede it is most clearly demonstrable in a handful of works. I share her concern about the slim corpus and the translation burden for Michon, which is why I place him third and not higher despite the compression and formal control. Where we differ is that I do not think scale alone should decide between Cărtărescu and Carson.

responses.point: Carlberg also ranks Carson first, for formal invention tied to intellectual depth and emotional force. She flags that Carson's translations of ancient texts sit at the edge of what counts as original literary work under Nobel's will, and that the text-only reading may miss book design and performance.
responses.response: I agree on both points and would not rest the citation on the translations. A prize for the whole oeuvre should name the original poetry, verse-novel and essay work. Because Nox in particular depends on its physical form, we should say openly that a text-only reading understates it. I would add a qualification to our shared view: agreement on Carson's ranking is not evidence of her merit, and the objection about specialist allusiveness narrowing her readership should be answered on the literary evidence and not set aside because several of us ranked her first.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and asks whether the hybrid formats will prove lasting in the canon or remain influential mainly among peers. She places Tawada third, for linguistic estrangement as a generative method, and notes that Tawada's international profile is more recent.
responses.response: Her question about lasting weight versus peer influence is the right test, and I cannot answer it with certainty. I would say the emotional force of Autobiography of Red and Nox gives them a claim beyond a specialist readership. On Tawada, I recognise that the linguistic achievement is central to her work and not incidental. I rank her lower mainly because I am less sure the lighter register and the wordplay survive translation at the scale a whole-oeuvre citation would require, and because I cannot judge her poetry and drama as well as her prose. That is a limit of my coverage, not a verdict on the work.

uncertainties: My assessment rests on general public knowledge of the major works and the supplied longlist summaries, not on a fresh reading or independent verification of the corpus.
It is unclear how a citation should separate Carson's original poetry, verse-novel and essays from her translations, adaptations and collaborative or visual projects.
It is unclear whether her most formally radical books carry enough weight, and whether the later work sustains the level of the central titles.
For Cărtărescu, Michon and Tawada, the quality of the original-language prose and the extent of translation coverage cannot be verified from the supplied evidence.
The committee has not settled how the will's 'ideal direction' applies to hybrid, allusive work compared with epic or visionary prose.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. His own literary practice is context only and not evidence of preference.
